items.title: llama-modchip claims DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284B MoE) runs CPU-only in 64 GB RAM at about 9-15 tok/s
items.summary: The open-source llama-modchip project (Apache-2.0) patches llama.cpp kernels and ships quantisation tools to run big MoE models from system RAM. Its README says DeepSeek-V4-Flash (284.33B total, 13.17B active) is quantised to 56.56 GiB at 1.71 bits per weight, peaking at 57.61 GiB RSS at 256K context. It reports 44.36 tok/s prefill and 9.06-14.7 tok/s decode on a Ryzen 9 9955HX with 64 GB DDR5.
items.why_it_matters: If the claims hold, a frontier-scale open-weight MoE runs on a high-end laptop with no GPU. Quality at 1.71 bits is untested, and the custom tensor format does not load in stock llama.cpp.

sources.title: llama-modchip: CPU-First Inference for 284B & 30B MoE Models

items.confidence_note: Self-reported README numbers only; no independent test. published_at is the Hacker News first-seen time (304 points), an estimate. The README is internally inconsistent on peak RSS (57.61 vs 58.9 GiB).

items.title: Video Rebirth's HyperFlow H3 Flash shrinks MiniMax-H3 video model from about 31B to about 14B parameters for 4-8 step generation
items.summary: Video Rebirth published HyperFlow H3 Flash on GitHub, a pruned, low-rank-factorised and INT8-quantised derivative of MiniMax-H3 with 13.7-13.9B parameters versus about 31B. It runs in 4, 6 (default) or 8 steps without classifier-free guidance. Self-reported timings are 8.7 s for a 5.2 s clip on 4x B200, 36 s on one H200 and 92 s on one RTX 5090.
items.why_it_matters: Third parties are turning an open-weight video model into one that fits consumer GPUs. The licence reportedly excludes the US, EU, UK and South Korea without MiniMax's authorisation.
items.confidence_note: Single primary source (README); speeds are self-reported. published_at estimated from the Hacker News listing (75 points, first seen 2026-11-07T18:02Z). Licence reading is from the README via a subagent.

learn.title: Size a quantised MoE's memory, and test a 'fits in 64 GB' claim
learn.why_today: The llama-modchip README claims a 284.33B-parameter MoE at 1.71 bits per weight fits in 64 GB, which is a checkable arithmetic claim.
learn.explanation: Weight memory is parameters times bits per weight divided by 8, so 284.33B at 1.71 bpw is about 56.6 GiB, matching the README's 56.56 GiB. At 3 bits the same model needs about 99 GiB, so only extreme quantisation fits. In an MoE all experts must be resident, so memory scales with total parameters, but each decoded token reads only the active parameters. Decode is therefore memory-bandwidth-bound and tok/s is at most bandwidth divided by active-weight bytes. This ignores KV cache, dequantisation compute and routing cache misses, and says nothing about quality loss at 1.71 bits.
learn.python:
# Illustrative numbers: weight memory for a MoE at a given bits-per-weight (bpw).
def weight_gib(params_b, bpw):
    return params_b * 1e9 * bpw / 8 / 2**30

def fits(total_b, bpw, ram_gib, kv_gib, os_gib=3.0):
    need = weight_gib(total_b, bpw) + kv_gib + os_gib
    return need, need <= ram_gib

for bpw in (16, 8, 4, 3, 1.71):
    need, ok = fits(284.33, bpw, 64, kv_gib=1.0)
    print(f"{bpw:>5} bpw: weights {weight_gib(284.33,bpw):7.1f} GiB, total {need:7.1f} GiB, fits 64 GiB: {ok}")
# Decode is memory-bound: each token reads the ACTIVE weights once.
active_b, bpw, bw_gbs = 13.17, 1.71, 90.0   # assumed DDR5 bandwidth, GB/s
bytes_tok = active_b * 1e9 * bpw / 8
print(f"upper bound decode: {bw_gbs*1e9/bytes_tok:.1f} tok/s at {bw_gbs} GB/s")
